scenes.title: Written Style and the Style of Debate
scenes.summary: Each kind of speech has its own style, and the written style is not that of debate. The written style is the most precise; the style of debate is the most suited to delivery, whether it shows character or emotion. Poets written for reading, like Chaeremon and Licymnius, are carried about in people's hands; writers' speeches seem thin in debate, and orators' amateurish on the page.

scenes.title: Repetition and Asyndeton
scenes.summary: What suits delivery seems silly without it. Repetition must be varied, as the actor Philemon varied “Rhadamanthus and Palamedes” in Anaxandrides' Old Men's Madness; asyndeta must be acted, and they amplify, making one thing many, as Homer makes Nireus memorable by naming him three times, though he mentions him once.

scenes.title: The Styles of the Three Kinds
scenes.summary: Speaking to the assembly is like shadow-painting: the larger the crowd, the more precision is wasted. The judicial style is more precise, above all before a single judge, where there is least room for rhetoric. The epideictic style, which is meant to be read, is the most suited to writing; the judicial comes second.

scenes.title: No Further Distinctions
scenes.summary: To add that style should be pleasant or magnificent is superfluous: the excellence already defined, clarity and appropriateness, with a good blend of the usual and the unfamiliar, rhythm, and the persuasiveness of the appropriate, will make it pleasant. So much for style; arrangement remains.
